title: Domino and Tromino Tiling
statement:
A board has 2 rows and `n` columns. Two kinds of tiles are available in unlimited supply, and each may be rotated freely:

- a **domino**, a straight piece covering 2 neighbouring cells;
- a **tromino**, an L-shaped piece covering 3 of the 4 cells of a 2 by 2 square.

Count the ways to cover every cell of the board with tiles that do not overlap and do not stick out of the board, and return the count modulo `10^9 + 7`. Two tilings count as different exactly when some pair of side-by-side cells is covered by one single tile in one of them but not in the other.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every placement of pieces works for tiny boards but the count grows roughly like 2.2 to the power n. Instead, build the board left to right. After placing pieces, the right edge is either flat (every column filled) or has a single cell sticking out into the next column. Those two shapes are all we need to remember: let `full[i]` count tilings of the first `i` columns, and `partial[i]` count tilings of the first `i - 1` columns plus one chosen cell (say the top) of column `i`. The bottom version has the same count by mirror symmetry.

## Approach

1. Set `full[0] = 1` (the empty board) and `full[1] = 1` (one vertical domino); every `partial` starts at 0.
2. For each `i` from 2 to `n`, a flat edge at column `i` is reached by: a vertical domino after `full[i - 1]`, two stacked horizontal dominoes after `full[i - 2]`, or a tromino that fills a jagged edge, after either mirror of `partial[i - 1]` (hence the factor 2).
3. A jagged edge at column `i` is reached by: a horizontal domino on the jagged edge of the other mirror, `partial[i - 1]`, or a tromino placed on a flat edge, `full[i - 2]`.
4. Take every value modulo `MOD` and return `full[n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`. Start with `full = [1, 1, 0, 0]`, `partial = [0, 0, 0, 0]`.

- `i = 2`: `full[2] = 1 + 1 + 2·0 = 2`, `partial[2] = 0 + 1 = 1`.
- `i = 3`: `full[3] = 2 + 1 + 2·1 = 5`, `partial[3] = 1 + 1 = 2`.

The answer is `full[3] = 5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one constant-time update per column.
- Space: O(n) for the two arrays (two rolling variables would make it O(1)).

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting the factor 2: a jagged edge can stick out at the top or at the bottom.
- Two horizontal dominoes stacked over columns `i - 1` and `i` are a new tiling, but two vertical dominoes there are already counted by `full[i - 1]`; do not count them twice.
- Reduce modulo `10^9 + 7` at every step; the counts overflow 32-bit integers by `n = 30`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `full[i]` | tilings of the first `i` columns with a flat right edge |
| `partial[i]` | tilings of the first `i - 1` columns plus the top cell of column `i` |
| `i` | the column being completed |

narration.3: full[i] will count tilings of the first i columns that end with a flat edge.
narration.4: partial[i] will count tilings that leave one cell of column i sticking out.
narration.5: The empty board has exactly one tiling: place nothing.
narration.6: A single column can only hold one vertical domino.
narration.8: Build the counts column by column.
narration.9: A flat edge comes from a vertical domino, two horizontal dominoes, or a tromino closing either kind of jagged edge.
narration.10: A jagged edge comes from a horizontal domino on the opposite jagged edge or a tromino on a flat edge.
narration.12: The whole 2 by n board must end flat, so return full[n].
